rewritten_text:
But enough of this. I will begin my story: it is my final task, and I hope I have the strength to finish it. I have no crimes to record; my faults should be readily forgiven, for they came from poor judgment, not evil intentions. I believe few people would claim that wiser decisions or different behavior could have spared them the misfortunes that have overtaken me. My fate has been ruled by necessity, a dreadful necessity. It would have taken hands stronger than mine—stronger, I believe, than any human power—to break the thick, unbreakable chain that bound me, once alive with nothing but joy and always filled with a warm love of goodness, to misery that only death can end, and that death will now soon end. But I am losing myself; my story remains untold. I will pause briefly, wipe my clouded eyes, and try to escape this vague but crushing unhappiness of the present through the sharper emotions of the past.

I was born in England. My father was a nobleman. His own father died while he was young, and a weak mother raised him with every indulgence she thought appropriate for a wealthy man of his rank. He was sent to Eton and then to college, and from childhood he was free to spend large sums of money. From his earliest youth, therefore, he enjoyed the independence that a boy with such advantages invariably acquires at a public school.

These circumstances gave his passions deep soil in which to take root and flourish, as flowers or weeds according to their nature. Always allowed to make his own decisions, he developed a distinct character early, one whose varied qualities allowed a perceptive observer to recognize the beginnings of both virtues and misfortunes. His thoughtless extravagance led him to spend immense sums satisfying passing whims, which he dignified as passions because of their apparent intensity. This extravagance often took the form of boundless generosity. Yet even when he devoted himself sincerely to other people’s needs, his own desires were satisfied completely. He gave money without sacrificing any wish of his own; he gave his time, which he did not value, and his affection, which he was happy to have called upon in any way.

I do not mean that he would have shown excessive selfishness if his desires had conflicted with those of others. That test simply never came. He grew up surrounded by prosperity and all its advantages; everyone loved him and wanted to please him.

There was something strange in all this that fascinated and delighted me. It was as though he had finally woken from a long, dream-filled sleep. He felt rather like one of the seven sleepers, or like Nourjahad in that lovely imitation of an Eastern tale. Diana was gone; his friends had changed or died. Now, on waking, he had only me left in the world to love.

How precious the waters, mountains, and woods of Loch Lomond became to me, now that someone I loved so much shared my walks. With my father I explored every lovely place: the islands, the waterfalls sheltered by trees, the shaded paths, and the little valleys tangled with ferns and undergrowth. Talking with him expanded my thoughts. I felt newly created, full of the freshness and energy of a new being. Since his arrival, I seemed to have moved from a tiny patch of earth into a universe without limits for my imagination or understanding. Before, my life had been like a pleasant country stream, destined never to leave its native fields, but to sink quietly into the ground once its work was done and leave no trace. Now it seemed like a varied river flowing through a rich and lovely landscape, always changing and always beautiful. Alas, I did not know what desert lay ahead, what rocks would tear its waters, or what dreadful scene its waves would reflect in an even more twisted form. Life was radiant then. I was beginning to learn hope, and what brings the heart greater despair than hope destroyed?

Is it not strange that sorrow should follow such heavenly happiness so quickly? I drank from an enchanted cup, but beneath its lingering sweetness lay bitterness. My heart was filled with deep love, and that very depth and fullness made it peaceful. I never imagined that love could bring misery. Everyone must eventually learn that lesson, but few are forced to learn it as I did. I mourn those few short months of paradise now, and I always will. I broke no commandment, ate no apple, yet I was driven from it without mercy. Alas, my companion did, and his fall dragged me down with him. But I am straying from my story. Let suffering arrive when its time comes; at this point I can still speak of happiness.

We spent three months in this delightful companionship before my aunt became ill. I stayed in her room for an entire month, nursing her, but her illness was fatal. She died, and for some time nothing could comfort me. Death is so terrible to those left alive. The bonds of habit are powerful, even without affection to hold them together, and when they break the heart cannot help suffering.

The group split between two neighboring benches. Anne sat on the front one, and Mr. Elliot, with help from his friend Colonel Wallis, had arranged things cleverly enough to secure the seat beside her. Miss Elliot was perfectly content, surrounded by her cousins and receiving most of Colonel Wallis’s flattering attention.

Anne was in exactly the right mood to enjoy the evening’s entertainment. It gave her just enough to occupy her mind. She could respond to the tender music, enjoy the cheerful pieces, concentrate on the technical ones, and be patient with the dull ones. She had never enjoyed a concert more, at least during the first act. Near its end, in the pause after an Italian song, she explained its words to Mr. Elliot. They shared a concert program.

“That,” she said, “is roughly the sense—or rather the meaning—of the words. We certainly cannot speak of sense in an Italian love song. Anyway, it is as close to the meaning as I can manage, because I don’t claim to know the language. My Italian is very poor.”

“Yes, yes, I can see that. Clearly you know nothing about it. You merely know enough to translate these shortened Italian lines, with their words all rearranged, straight into clear, understandable, elegant English. You need say no more about your ignorance. This proves it completely.”

“I won’t argue with such kind politeness. Still, I would be sorry to have a true expert test me.”

“I haven’t been enjoying visits to Camden Place all this time,” he replied, “without learning something about Miss Anne Elliot. I consider her too modest for most people to recognize even half her talents, and so talented that modesty would be impossible for any other woman.”

“For shame! That is far too much flattery. I have forgotten what comes next,” she said, turning to the program.

“Perhaps,” Mr. Elliot said quietly, “I have known about your character longer than you realize.”

“Really? How could that be? You can only have known about me since I came to Bath, unless you heard my family speak of me before.”

“I knew of you by reputation long before you came to Bath. People who knew you well had described you to me. I have known what you were like for many years. Your appearance, your nature, your talents, your manner—I already knew about them all.”

Mr. Elliot succeeded in stirring the interest he had hoped to arouse. No one can resist the attraction of a mystery like that.
